10826-the-book-bills-of-narcissus-an-acc:
Richard Le Gallienne rendered The Book-Bills of Narcissus in 1895, a fanciful account of a book lover's debts and dreams. Chapters run from introductory musings through Narcissus opening his Gladstone, accounts rendered, an idyll of Alice Sunshine, the Sibylline books, and the children of Apollo. A frontispiece by Robert Fowler decorates the volume.

Le Gallienne writes of books as loves and luxuries, with wit and a poet's feeling for bindings, bargains, and borrowers. The book suits bibliophiles who know the ache of wanting one more volume. Readers get a light, bookish pleasure, dedicated to a lost love named Mildred.
15258-cecilia-de-noe-l:
Lanoe Falconer's Cecilia de Noël, in a 1910 Macmillan edition, opens after dinner in a drawing-room, where Atherley preaches a gospel of science. Closed shutters, shaded lamps, a wood fire, and hothouse flowers make a mild twilight, while Atherley claims science satisfies all reasonable desires. Bread, not manna, is his test.

Cecilia herself, a figure of mystery and grace, soon challenges that gospel of fact with something stranger and kinder. Falconer writes in a subtle, literary style, probing faith, reason, and ghostly wonder. Readers who like quiet, thoughtful ghost tales will find the novel delicate and haunting.
15651-his-grace-of-osmonde-being-the-por:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this historical romance, His Grace of Osmonde, in New York in 1914, from Charles Scribner's Sons, illustrated, copyrighted in 1897. The subtitle explains the conceit: the portions of that nobleman's life omitted in his lady's story, presented to the world of fashion as A Lady of Quality. An epigraph pleads for justice and mercy, since Nature is unjust to man from his first hour.

Contents open on the fifth day of April, 1676, with he is the king, Sir Jeoffry Wildairs, and God have mercy on its evil fortunes. My lord marquess plunges into the Thames, and a lady writes of scandal. Sir John Oxon lays a wager at Cribb's coffee house, my lord rides to Camylott, and a portrait is sold. Burnett writes a Restoration romance of courts, wagers, and wild heirs, told from the duke's side of a famous love story.
16323-the-continental-monthly-vol-4-no-4:
Volume four, number four of The Continental Monthly, dated October 1863, mixes war, letters, and money in a Northern monthly. Contents list The Freedom of the Press, The Brothers, and William Lilly Astrologer. A piece on Jefferson Davis, repudiation, recognition, and slavery follows. The diary of Frances Krasinska, Thirty Days with the Seventy-First Regiment, and Currency and the National Finances close the number. A detective's story, literary notices, and poems fill out the number.

Its lead essay on press freedom tackles government suppression of papers during the war, a live and bitter question. The magazine's blend of policy and fiction marks it as a serious Civil War monthly. Readers will find a varied, argumentative issue from the war's middle years.
17119-the-vision-of-sir-launfal-and-othe:
James Russell Lowell's Riverside volume pairs a life sketch of the poet with his best-loved verse. The Vision of Sir Launfal leads, a Grail quest in two parts with preludes, where a knight learns that true holiness lies in humble kindness, not in grand quests. An ode for Harvard, an Indian-summer reverie, the first snow-fall, and poems to Garrison and Phillips follow.

Notes and a portrait aid students, and the set shows Lowell as poet, critic, and public man. His verse mixes nature, faith, and reform in clear, musical lines. Readers new to Lowell will find this a fine first book, with his most famous poem at its head and his range close behind.
17948-the-vision-of-sir-launfal-and-othe:
James Russell Lowell wrote The Vision of Sir Launfal, and this school edition, edited by Julian W. Abernethy, was printed in New York in 1908 for Merrill's English Texts. Abernethy adds a life of Lowell, notes, and tributes from other poets, so pupils could read the verse with help at hand.

The title poem sends a knight in search of the Holy Grail, only to learn that true grace lies in humble kindness at home. Other poems include The Shepherd of King Admetus, a railroad car incident, and an ode to the dandelion. It is a fine schoolbook of American verse, still loved for its music and its gentle moral.
18176-yorkshire-tales-third-series-amusi:
John Hartley, author of the Clock Almanack and Yorkshire Ditties, wrote this third series of Yorkshire tales in the Yorkshire dialect. The sketches use local speech throughout, with verses that urge readers to meet good and bad folk with song rather than worry, and to forgive and forget. Hartley published the volume in London with William Nicholson and Sons.

Contents include Grimes' New Hat, Sammywell Sweeps the Chimley, Hepsabah's Hat, Old Dave to the New Parson, Sammywell's Eggsperiment, and True Blue, a romance of factory life. Later sketches add a bashful Bradfordian, a fish shop, a bull pup, and Christmas oysters. Readers get Yorkshire humor in its own voice, full of mills, chapels, and village talk.
18977-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-1:
This volume of The Continental Monthly gathers its first year, 1862, a magazine devoted to literature and national policy. Published in Boston and New York, it opened in the early months of the Civil War, when the Union's cause and conduct were under fierce debate. Its index shows the range: travel writing, war reporting, fiction, and historical essays.

Contributors include Horace Greeley on travel across the continent, Edmund Kirke on the pines and the war, and C. G. Leland on early discoverers of America. Literature and politics share the pages by design. Readers get a full year of Northern magazine writing from the war's first year, valuable for its arguments, stories, and sense of a nation at war.
1907-rowdy-of-the-cross-l:
B. M. Sinclair, also known as B. M. Bower, tells of Rowdy Vaughan, christened Rowland by his mother and rechristened by the range. He is lost in a blizzard and refused shelter by Miss Conroy. Rowdy hires a new boss, joins the Cross L ranch, and works his way up through shots in the dark, tough places, and a threatening mood from his friend Pink.

The chapters follow Rowdy from blizzard to promotion, with Harry Conroy at home and Jessie waiting at the story's edge. Bower writes the ranch novel with humor and pace, and Rowdy himself — stubborn, loyal, and quick with a grin — is one of her most likable heroes.
19415-libraries-in-the-medieval-and-rena:
J. W. Clark, registrary of Cambridge, gave this Rede Lecture in June of eighteen ninety-four, with lantern slides to show his points. He asks whether a library is a workshop for readers or a museum for treasures, and argues that the practical view best serves learning.

The lecture traces how great religious houses, finding their books too many for old rooms, built special libraries, often over existing halls, in the fourteen hundreds. It is a short, clear history of library buildings, still cited by students of books and reading.
21077-the-mind-and-the-brain-being-the-a:
Alfred Binet, director of the psychology laboratory at the Sorbonne, wrote the work translated here as The Mind and the Brain. First issued in French as L'Âme et le Corps, it appeared in English in London in 1907 in the International Scientific Series. Binet asks what matter is and how the mind can know it.

His first book argues that we know the outer world only through our sensations. The nervous system, he says, stands between the self and everything outside it. Later parts take up the nature of mind itself. The book shows a leading early psychologist wrestling with old questions in plain, careful terms.
23747-destruction-and-reconstruction-per:
Richard Taylor, lieutenant-general in the Confederate Army, published Destruction and Reconstruction in 1879, recording his personal experiences of secession, war, and reconstruction. He writes as an actor in the events, who enjoyed exceptional advantages for an interior view, and he tells readers plainly that his opinions are sincerely held but open to their judgment.

Chapters move from secession and the Charleston convention through Manassas, the Peninsula campaign, and the Louisiana brigade known as the Tigers. Taylor names Bragg, Johnston, Jefferson Davis, and Alexander Stephens among the figures he knew. Where his facts rest on weaker authority, he says, his language will show it. Readers new to the war will find his plain style easy to follow. His chapters move in the order the events happened. The book remains a leading Confederate memoir.
23826-a-sketch-of-the-life-of-the-late-h:
William Cooper wrote A Sketch of the Life of the Late Henry Cooper, barrister-at-law of the Norfolk circuit, and of his father, published in London. His dedication, dated December 1856, goes to Mr. Sergeant Storks, who knew Henry well on circuit and often opposed him in court, and who could best appreciate his talents and eloquence.

For years Henry worked at the bar with almost no recognition, until his brilliance came to notice and his great ability won acknowledgement. No sooner had he reached that eminence, with all made easy before him, than death cut his thread of life. Cooper asks the reader's indulgence for a brother's memoir, written with affection and with a lawyer's eye for character.
24531-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-4:
Published in October 1862, this fourth number of the second volume of The Continental Monthly was devoted to literature and national policy. Its leading piece takes up the slogan, The Constitution as it is, the Union as it was, a pet phrase in some quarters since the rebellion broke out.

The writer argues that such cries carry great power over unreflecting crowds, and that the phrase can bear both a good, loyal sense and a dangerous one. Other pieces treat the war's politics and letters. The issue shows educated Northern readers arguing over the Union's meaning in the war's second year.
24982-the-continental-monthly-vol-3-no-1:
The January 1863 number of The Continental Monthly, volume three, published in New York by John F. Trow, carries the magazine's double charge of literature and national policy into the Civil War's middle year. Contents include the Huguenots of New Rochelle, a tenth installment of Maccaroni and Canvas, Consequences of the Rebellion, and The Union, comparing New York and Virginia. Fiction, poetry, and survey work share the pages.

Charles Godfrey Leland's The Ivy retells how Kissos, a young faun beloved by Bacchus, danced until he fell dead at an orgy. His grieving lord changed him into ivy, wreathed around his brow. A companion nymph, Kiseis, who helped raise the infant Bacchus, was placed among the stars for her reward. The number shows a wartime magazine balancing argument, story, and classical fancy.
27113-narrative-of-a-voyage-to-india-of-:
W. B. Cramp's 1823 Narrative of a Voyage to India follows his sailing in the Princess Charlotte, Indiaman, from January 1815. The ship takes cargo at North-fleet Hope, sails with Company ships from Gravesend, and waits at the Downs while storms drive the Tarva onto the Goodwin Sands.

Later sections tell of a shipwreck on board the Lady Castlereagh and give a description of New South Wales. Cramp records the crossing-the-line ceremony, the arrival at Madras, and the daily life of an East India voyage in plain, seamanlike prose.
27183-the-gate-of-appreciation-studies-i:
Carleton Noyes's The Gate of Appreciation, published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1907, studies the relation of art to life. It opens with a traveler in wild country at evening, wind chilling and rain threatening, who feels the need of shelter and gathers scattered stones to hand.

Later chapters take up the attitude of response, technique and the layman, the value of the medium, the service of criticism, and beauty and common life. Noyes shows how Winslow Homer's breakers bring back salt fragrance and stinging spray, arguing that the senses, trained by art, deepen our enjoyment of the world.
31910-memoirs-of-the-extraordinary-milit:
John Shipp's Memoirs of the Extraordinary Military Career, in a new illustrated edition of 1890 with an introduction by H. Manners Chichester, were written by Shipp himself, late a lieutenant in His Majesty's 87th Regiment. Chichester notes that Shipp claimed birth on March 16, 1785, at Saxmundham in Suffolk, though the parish register records his baptism twelve months earlier.

Shipp, second son of Thomas and Laetitia Shipp, lost his mother young, entered the parish poorhouse, and passed to a neighboring farmer, a savage taskmaster of the good old times. Then the French Revolutionary War offered deliverance. Readers get a soldier's autobiography of the Napoleonic age, from poorhouse boy to officer, told with adventure-series gusto.
3275-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part five of Artemus Ward's complete works holds his London Punch letters. Ward, the American showman-humorist, wrote for Punch during his visit to London, and the letters report England back to itself through American eyes. London sights, London manners, and London pride all pass under his misspelled gaze.

The humor lies in the mismatch: a Yankee showman loose among empire's ceremonies, spelling badly and seeing clearly. Ward flatters no one, least of all himself, and his letters delighted both sides of the Atlantic. The letters delighted both sides of the Atlantic, and they still read as a showman's postcards home.
34067-catholic-churchmen-in-science-firs:
James J. Walsh wrote these sketches of the lives of Catholic ecclesiastics who were among the great founders in science. A second edition appeared in Philadelphia in 1910 by the Dolphin Press, with copyright in 1906 and 1910. Walsh, dean and professor of medicine at Fordham and professor of physiological psychology at Cathedral College, New York, dedicates the book to the memory of his mother.

The preface notes that the sketches appeared at various times during the past five years in Catholic magazines, written because the material deserved wider notice. Walsh shows priests and churchmen at the heart of early science. The book serves readers who want faith and science told together.
36270-the-gospel-of-evolution-from-the-a:
The Gospel of Evolution is a lecture by Edward Aveling from a freethought series. The Freethought Publishing Company issued it in London in 1884. The series title was The Atheistic Platform, twelve lectures in all. Aveling proclaims a new and better gospel now preached to men. The old gospel, he argues, is neither news nor good. Nineteen centuries of preaching have made it old, he says.

Worse, he holds, it lacks the inherent life of reality. Its tales of the past mislead, its hopes and threats deceive. The angels' song of peace on earth was, for Aveling, a false alarm. The scientific gospel of evolution offers instead a universal brotherhood. Aveling warns his own side not to make an idol of one idea. Evolution, a generalisation of generalisations, tempts men to just that error.
38143-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume twelve slice four, runs from Grasshopper to Greek Language. The title page calls the work a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Transcriber notes explain the marks for subscripts, roots, and Greek letters, and list small printing errors set right.

The article list mixes nature, men, and places: Grass of Parnassus, Gratian, Grattan, Thomas Gray, Graz, and a grayling. Great set pieces on Greece, Greek art, and the Greek language anchor the slice. Reference hunters get Edwardian learning in compact form, entry by entry.
39305-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de:
The Memoirs of Jacques Casanova de Seingalt, covering 1725 to 1798, are here in volume five of six, covering London and Moscow. The text is the rare unabridged London edition of 1894, translated by Arthur Machen. Chapters discovered by Arthur Symons are added. A caution warns the memoirs were not written for children.

Contents list episodes, not plain chapters. The south of France, the road to London, the English episode, a flight from London to Berlin, and Russia and Poland make the volume map. The text opens at Genoa. A man there called himself Possano, and presented a wife and daughter so ugly that Casanova left on a trifling pretext. Readers get Casanova later travels, at full indiscreet length.
39894-roman-sepulchral-inscriptions-thei:
John Kenrick reads Roman grave stones for what they tell of speech, faith, and daily life in a London volume dated M DCCC LVIII. John Russell Smith in Soho Square and York sellers shared the printing. A stone from a sarcophagus in the York Museum fronts the title page with a child's brief record.

Kenrick states that the work grew from two papers read to the Yorkshire Philosophical Society. He aimed to draw eyes to stones kept in their own museum and to link the antiquary's work with manners and belief. Contents treat graves outside town walls, words to travellers, and warnings to those who would break a tomb. Later heads cover trades, tools on tombs, length of life, and praise for wives, parents, and children.
40067-the-iron-boys-on-the-ore-boats-or-:
James R Mears wrote a boys' adventure copyrighted in 1913, one of a series about the Iron Boys in mines and steel mills. Steve Rush and Bob Jarvis take a new job as inspectors and then as ordinary seamen on ore boats. Bob doubts he will like leaving good pay and bossing in the mines. Steve calls the change a great chance to add to their store of knowledge.

Chapters promise trouble in the stoke hole, a crash in the fog, and a tragedy of the lakes. Steve saves the captain, and both boys take turns at the wheel. A wireless message and an exciting rescue come near the end.
4051-lady-bridget-in-the-never-never-lan:
Rosa Praed's Australian novel of 1915 tells of Lady Bridget O'Hara, an Irishwoman who marries into the harsh world of Queensland's Never-Never land. The story is told in three books, first through Mrs. Gildea, then through Bridget herself, then through Colin McKeith and others.

Bridget's engagement to Colin McKeith raises hard questions of settlements and capital, since he needs all his money for wells and cattle. Praed writes of station life, heat, and social rank with a settler's eye. Readers who enjoy Australian sagas of love and land will find a rich, old-fashioned romance of the outback.
40646-a-history-of-spain-founded-on-the-:
Charles Chapman's A History of Spain, founded on the Historia de Espana of Rafael Altamira, was published by Macmillan in New York in 1918. Chapman, an assistant professor of history at the University of California, gives the book to his son Seville Dudley Chapman, born in the city whose name he bears. A map of Spain and Portugal, compiled by Chapman, stands at the front.

Geography comes first, for its grip on Spanish history. Then the early peoples to 206 BC, Roman Spain, and Visigothic Spain. Moslem Spain runs from 711, with Christian Spain beside it, and the era of the Spanish crusades follows. Castile and Aragon grow toward national unity in parallel chapters, and the Catholic Kings close the run of the contents kept here.
41508-seven-legs-across-the-seas-a-print:
Seven Legs Across the Seas, a printer's impressions of many lands, is a travel book by Samuel Murray. Murray, also the author of From Clime to Clime, printed it at New York in 1918. He tells how he boarded a fast ship and headed south through New York harbour toward Sandy Hook. He had bought a second class ticket to Buenos Aires by way of England.

That sailing was the first of several legs of a trip round the world he had planned. The sum he thought needful was thirteen hundred and fifty dollars, saved by years of frugal living. By trade he was a printer and linotype operator. In earlier years he had beaten his way about the country on freight trains, riding box cars and guarding his eyes from the cinders of engines. The book joins a working man's craft to a wanderer's tale.
41962-law-of-the-north-originally-publis:
Law of the North, a story of love and battle in Rupert's Land, was first published under the title Empery. Samuel Alexander White wrote it, and Grosset and Dunlap reissued it at New York from the Outing edition of 1913. The contents open with the breed of the north.

A lodge in the wilderness, an ultimatum, and omens of the law follow. Desiree, in the blood, and lieges of the wild fill the middle chapters. The tale begins with Basil Dreaulond, a courier of the Hudson's Bay Company, hiding his pack in a tamarack thicket at a sound. White wrote of the fur trade's last wars, when company men and free traders fought for the north. His novel mixes romance with the hard law of the wilds.
42048-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, is the famous 1911 encyclopaedia, and this text is the volume running from Lefebvre to a later letter of the alphabet. The transcriber's notes explain the handling of subscripts, superscripts, and side notes in this copy. Side notes stand as titles of their paragraphs. Greek letters and roots are spelled out in brackets.

The notes list misprints corrected in the articles, among them pieces on Legge, on the bean family, and on Leibnitz. The eleventh edition is famed for scholarship written in clear prose by experts. This volume covers names and subjects across the letter L and beyond.
42299-the-history-of-johnny-qu-genus-the:
History of Johnny Qua Genus is a comic poem with Rowlandson plates. Methuen of London issued this new edition in nineteen o three. It rests on the Ackermann edition of eighteen twenty two in print. Twenty four coloured pictures by Thomas Rowlandson light the verse tale.

Johnny is the little foundling of the late Doctor Syntax books by the author. The Tours of Doctor Syntax had won such favour that a sequel followed. The foundling is led through a varied track of life in the poem. The writer aimed at an English Gil Blas in this small volume. Rowlandson pencil gives the scenes their usual comic felicity and life.
42708-woman-under-monasticism-chapters-o:
Woman Under Monasticism, chapters on saint-lore and convent life between the years 500 and 1500, by Lina Eckenstein, was printed at Cambridge in 1896. Eckenstein dedicates the book to her friends Karl and Maria Sharpe Pearson. A Latin motto holds that the life of spiritual men without letters is death. Her preface frames the study in the unrest of a changing age.

Old standards are now questioned, she notes, and the past must be read to judge the present. Monastic life across ten centuries, she argues, fed some of the most peaceful and forward trends of the Middle Ages. For women, the convent above all fostered the best sides of mind, morals, and feeling, and shaped women's schooling for ages. The book mixes saint tales with social history.
43331-the-domestic-life-of-thomas-jeffer:
The Domestic Life of Thomas Jefferson, compiled from family letters and reminiscences by his great-granddaughter Sarah Randolph, was published by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1871. A portrait after Gilbert Stuart and a view of Monticello's western front illustrate the volume, with Jefferson's seal.

Randolph states her object in the preface. She will not show Jefferson the great man or the statesman, but Jefferson in private life. Hers is the warm domestic character described by those who knew and loved him best. Her materials are the reminiscences written by his daughter and grandchildren. Family letters culled from his correspondence, published and unpublished, she calls the most faithful witnesses of the warmth of his affections. She acknowledges Randall's three-volume Life as the chief authority, offering instead a briefer view of the whole career.
43385-macmillan-co-s-catalogue-september:
Macmillans Catalogue of Works in Belles Lettres is the sales list of that house for September of eighteen seventy-four. It holds verse, tales, and like works, in ranks by the names of their hands. Each row gives the form, the cloth, and the price of the book. Short notes of praise from the press sheets of the day stand past most rows.

A long verse tale of Ireland opens the list, with praise for its point and plain grace. The full verse works of a famed poet stand in two parts at a set price. An art tour of the north chief towns takes praise for its mix of fact and light tale. A boys sea tale by a famed trek man is in its fifth print. The list is a shot of what one great house sold to the read world of its day.
44974-a-short-account-of-the-extraordina:
A short life written by its own subject tells of a man born in St Domingo who was held as a prisoner of war at Ashbourn in Derbyshire. He paid one shilling for the printed tale, which was sold at Ashbourn, London, and Derby. His name is given only in short form on the title page.

He frames his hard road as a sign of God's care and of his turn to faith. Loss of wealth, war, and jail all test him, and he warns readers not to trust in riches. He expects scorn for his tale and leaves its worth, he says, to God to judge.
45162-how-to-travel-hints-advice-and-sug:
How to Travel is a guide book of hints for roamers by Thomas Knox. The author had roamed Asia and wrote a shelf of tour books for boys. His full title claims hints for travel by land and sea all over the globe. The book came out in the year eighteen eighty one.

Pack lists, fare tricks, health rules, and port forms fill its parts. Drug dose signs in the text serve sick roamers far from a doctor. Ads for tour gear in the book have been moved to its end in this text. A warm gift page sends the book to all who roam land or sea. The tone is brisk and sure, from a man who had seen the world.
46602-lydia-knight-s-history-the-first-b:
Lydia Knight's History opens the Noble Women's Lives Series, printed at the Juvenile Instructor Office in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1883. The author signs as Homespun, and the publisher frames the book for young readers among the Saints. A preface cites demand for home literature after the Faith-Promoting Series pleased readers.

Lydia, the preface says, joined the Church early and stayed faithful through the trials of the first Saints. Chapter one shows her as a small fair haired girl pulling wool from a sheepskin in a forest clearing in western New York. Born in 1812 at Sutton in Worcester County, Massachusetts, she had moved west with her family two years before. Her father Jesse Goldthwait is drawn as prudent, hard working, and firm.
47947-self-knowledge-and-guide-to-sex-in:
Professor T W Shannon wrote Self Knowledge and Guide to Sex Instruction, dated nineteen thirteen, a book on the vital facts of life. Shannon lectured on moral and reform topics and sat on the board of the World's Purity Federation. The book was sold only by its Ohio publisher.

The title page promises a full guide for parents teaching their children. It offers timely help for boys and girls at the ages of greatest danger. Warnings name pitfalls hidden in their path. Counsel for the married of all ages follows, with a word on the laws of sex and heredity. Special chapters come from Stanley Finch and Charles W Eliot. Purity is the book's ruling aim.
49154-life-of-a-scotch-naturalist-thomas:
Samuel Smiles wrote the Life of a Scotch Naturalist, the biography of Thomas Edward, published by John Murray in London in 1877 and here in its fourth edition. Smiles, the author of Self-Help and Lives of the Engineers, had cited Edward in Self-Help eighteen years before. He calls him one of the most extraordinary instances of perseverance in science he ever met.

Edward was a shoemaker, and a shoemaker still when the book appeared. For nearly thirty years he fought the battle of scientific poverty, living for science, not by it. Too shy to push himself forward, he was almost forgotten when his work was done. Smiles tells how Edward satisfied his thirst for knowledge amid domestic poverty, spending most nights out of doors in damp and wet. The life became a classic of its kind.
4957-the-heart-s-secret-or-the-fortunes-:
Lieutenant Murray Ballou's Heart's Secret follows a soldier's fortunes through love, war, and exile, beginning with an accident and a sudden introduction to a belle. Chapters carry him among Cuban banditti, through wounding, challenge, imprisonment, and a farewell, toward banishment, promotion, and an audience with a queen.

The locale is a gem of the American archipelago, and the story moves between battlefield and ballroom with melodramatic energy. Unrequited love, disguise, an assassin, and a final avowal complete the arc. Readers get a swashbuckling romance of the Spanish-American world, written for those who like their soldiers brave and their endings happy.
50555-bibliographic-notes-on-one-hundred:
Notes on one hundred books famous in English literature make up this reference work. The long note at the front warns readers about the print of old books. In those books the long s looks like an f, and w was often printed as vv. The letters u and v change places, as do i and j, in the old spelling.

The note explains that folk once wrote words as they heard them, so spellings shift from page to page. Marks and stops fall where a modern reader would not expect them. A list of corrections stands at the end of the book, on page 221. Readers of old texts get a plain guide to these quirks before they start.
51097-heroines-of-mormondom-the-second-b:
Heroines of Mormondom is the second book of the Noble Women Lives series, printed in 1884. The Juvenile Instructor office at Salt Lake City published the volume for the Saints. A preface hopes the lives will prove no less interesting than the first book. Lessons in the articles should instruct the youth of this people, it adds.

Remarkable events in the sketches will strengthen faith and love for the gospel, it says. Such women suffered much with noble men for their faith in the early church. No age or nation, the preface claims, shows finer examples of female heroism. Mormon girls gained pioneer mothers as patterns in these short life sketches.
53191-william-jennings-bryan-a-concise-b:
William Jennings Bryan: A Concise But Complete Story of His Life and Services is a campaign biography by Harvey Newbranch. It was published in 1900 at Lincoln, Nebraska, by the University Publishing Company. The book is dedicated to Bryan as the brave and patriotic leader of an honest and intelligent body of voters.

The contents run from an introduction and Bryan's early life to his years in Congress. Whole chapters treat the tariff question and the rise of the silver issue, the cause that made his name. Then come chapters on the presidential candidate, on new issues, and on his renomination. A long chapter gives his speech at Indianapolis. The book closes with Bryan the man and his home life. It is a supporter's full portrait of the Nebraska leader at the height of his second run for the presidency.
5337-thirty-one-years-on-the-plains-and-:
Captain William F. Drannan's Thirty-One Years on the Plains and in the Mountains, subtitled The Last Voice from the Plains, records a lifetime of hunting, trapping, scouting, and Indian fighting in the Far West. Drannan went to the plains at fifteen, and his preface warns that he makes no attempt at romance or great literary production, but narrates in his own plain, blunt way.

The book offers a first-hand account of frontier life, from trapping and scouting to warfare with Native peoples, told by a man who lived it. Readers will find a vivid, if one-sided, record of the West as its old trappers remembered it, before the frontier closed.
56042-discovery-of-the-yosemite-and-the-:
Discovery of the Yosemite is a memoir by Lafayette Bunnell, a doctor and soldier. Revell issued the third edition, revised and corrected. Bunnell served with the Mariposa Battalion. That unit entered the Yosemite valley in 1851. An Indian war of that year led to the entry. The book is told by one of the discoverers himself. A portrait and a list of views open the volume.

The plates name the valley's great sights. El Capitan, Half Dome, and Bridal Veil Fall appear. Mirror Lake, Sentinel Rock, and the big trees follow. Acorn storehouses of the Indians are also shown. Bunnell later served as a surgeon in the Civil War. His tale mixes war, wonder, and the naming of places. It remains a first account of a famed valley. Few discovery stories rest on such an eyewitness.
56053-the-day-of-doom-or-a-poetical-desc:
Michael Wigglesworth, teacher of the church at Malden in New England, wrote The Day of Doom in 1662. This printing follows the sixth edition of 1715. A memoir of the author and a sketch of his funeral sermon by Cotton Mather are included.

The long poem describes the great and last judgment in verse, with Bible texts at its head. For more than a century, the memoir says, no poetry was more popular in New England. Children learned it with their catechisms, and hawkers sold it on sheets like ballads. Its terrors picture the wrath of an offended God on the day of doom.
56605-madame-de-stae-l:
Madame de Stael is a life of the great maid of pens of that name by Bella Duffy. It stands in a set of lives of famed women. That set is list at the front, with the lives of maids of tale, of song, and of the stage. It was put out at Boston in eighteen eighty seven. A first word at the front treats the stuff of such a life.

Notes of her own hand, left in no print, are not to be had in this case, that word says. That want is the loss of each keen man who would write her life. The house of her kin, it is well known, burnt or hid those notes. In their place the hand must use the notes of the men and maids of her age.
56743-larry-dexter-and-the-stolen-boy-or:
Howard R Garis wrote Larry Dexter and the Stolen Boy, a tale for boys put out in New York in 1912. Its short title calls Larry a young news man on the lakes. A plate shows Larry who shoves a man hard back to a wall, at page 198. Garis had told past tales of Larry as a news boy and on a great search.

The tale opens in the city room of the New York Leader one day in the fall. Paul Rosberg, one of the old hands of that sheet, greets Larry with warmth. He says Larry is just the lad he had hoped to see that day. A lost boy, a hunt by boat and by shore, and the craft of news work drive the plot.
57119-an-account-of-the-life-and-writing:
An Account of the Life and Writings of Irenaeus is a work of church history by James Beaven, of Saint Edmund Hall, Oxford, published in London by Rivington in 1841. Irenaeus was bishop of Lyons and a martyr of the second century. Beaven meant the book to show the doctrine and discipline of the early church.

Twenty-one chapters lay out the evidence. After the life and writings come chapters on the Trinity, the origin of evil, evil spirits, and the canon and use of scripture. Baptism, the Eucharist, justification, ceremonies, and the Sabbath receive their own treatments. A final account treats the Gnostic heretics, from Simon Magus and Saturninus to Marcion. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
58601-hiking-westward-being-the-story-of:
Roger Conant wrote Hiking Westward for the Wilde Company of Boston, copyrighted in 1920, with pictures by Merrill. Its subtitle tells the plot: two boys whose ambition led them to face privations and hardships in their quest of a home in the great West.

The boys are Phil and Ted Porter, teased at the supper table because one thinks only of baseball and the other of a homemade flying machine. Their mother's question, what they would do if called to support the family, starts the adventure. Chapters take them by river and rapids toward Lake Superior, into a lumber camp, and out to a claim. There they build an irrigation plant, fight for their home, and end with a house-raising. Word from Washington and a fortunate discovery close the tale.
58716-the-day-of-doom-or-a-poetical-desc:
Michael Wigglesworth, teacher of the church at Malden in New England, wrote The Day of Doom in 1662. The poem describes the great and last judgment. This edition adds other poems, a memoir of the author, his autobiography, and a sketch of his funeral sermon by Cotton Mather.

The title page anchors the poem in scripture, quoting Acts on the day God will judge the world and Matthew on the sign of the Son of Man. Wigglesworth's verses turned judgment into rhymes generations of colonists memorised. Readers get the best-known poem of colonial America in a scholarly reprint with the author's life attached.
59367-guatemala-and-her-people-of-to-day:
Guatemala and Her People of To-Day is a travel and country study by Nevin O. Winter, published in Boston in 1909 as a companion to his Mexico and Her People of To-Day. The subtitle promises an account of the land, its history and its people, with chapters on Honduras. The book is illustrated from photographs by the author.

The contents show a full survey: the ancient land, the capital, the people, railways, monuments, and the republic's story. A pronunciation guide and a route map are printed at the front. A pronunciation guide for Spanish-American place names is printed at the front for English-speaking readers, and a map shows the author's route. The frontispiece is a portrait of President Cabrera, under whose long rule the Guatemala of 1909 was governed.
59533-secret-history-or-the-horrors-of-s:
An unnamed lady wrote Secret History, or The Horrors of St Domingo, in a series of letters addressed to Colonel Burr, the late vice-president of the United States. Bradford and Inskeep published the book at Philadelphia in 1808. The letters were written at Cape Francois, chiefly during the command of General Rochambeau. In her preface the author admits she collected the letters reluctantly, at her friends' urging.

The first letter describes the passage out. Forty days of sea-sickness, heat, and confinement were softened by agreeable fellow passengers. From that arrival the letters witness the collapse of French St Domingo. The former slaves of the colony fought their way to independence. Rochambeau's army answered with the acts the title calls horrors. The book is an early American account of the Haitian Revolution, written by a woman who lived inside its events and sent her record to a famous, disgraced reader.
60321-prisoners-of-war-in-britain-1756-t:
Francis Abell wrote this record of war prisoners held in Britain from 1756 to 1815, printed at London in 1914. Oxford University Press issued the book, with plates of prison ships and camps. Abell tells of French and other foes taken in Britain's long wars, and of how they lived.

Early chapters treat the swap of prisoners and life on the prison hulks. Later ones walk through the great depots: Norman Cross, Dartmoor, Perth, and Portchester. Tales of famed escapers, such as Tom Souville, break the grim run. Parole life in British towns gets long, rich treatment. The book saves a lost world of captive men. Their crafts and games fill many warm pages.
6050-the-roots-of-the-mountains-wherein-:
William Morris tells of the men of Burgdale, their friends, neighbors, foemen, and fellows in arms, in The Roots of the Mountains. His opening verses mourn the traveler hurried past a fair abode by iron road, longing to stay amid garden, hay, and changing shadows and feel part of the place.

Morris says he strove to win such rest with the leaves of this book. Chapters open on Burgstead and its folk, Face-of-god and his kindred, and talk of divers matters in the hall. The romance follows a dale community holding its ground, its customs, and its kin against foes from beyond the mountains.
60781-catalogue-of-standard-recitations-:
Catalogue of Standard Recitations, numbers 19 to 34, is a list book from Ivers and Company of Pearl Street, New York. It does not print the pieces themselves. It names what each small number holds, so buyers and teachers can pick pieces to speak aloud at school and public nights.

Number 19 alone lists verse and prose by Whittier, Thackeray, Lowell, and Macaulay, among many more. Titles range from Caesar Passing the Rubicon to Courage, Boy, Courage, with prices of twelve cents by mail. The catalogue shows the wide trade in recitation pieces, a mainstay of school and hall programs in its day.
67663-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for December nineteen twelve is the Yuletide sheet of that set. The Century house of Union Square in New York brought it out. Frank Scott led the firm, with Ellsworth and Donald Scott in next posts. Its name stands filed at the state mark shop in that year. Gift ads crowd the front leaves, as fits a Yuletide sheet of its age.

A gear firm ad vaunts its shop mark as worth more than a trade sign. That mark is inlaid in the wood, a pledge of worth in the ad words. A gift book on the cast of goods is held out in the same ad. Birth child heir goods are the frame of that front sell talk. The sheet text was set from this same month print of the set.
68023-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine bound its eighty-fifth volume, running from November 1912 to April 1913, at New York. The hosted text opens with the volume's index, which maps six months of the magazine. A series on the impeachment of Andrew Johnson runs through it in parts, from its causes to the president's defence.

Another series takes up the Alaska bargain, Alaska as a territory of the United States. Henry Watterson writes on the humour and tragedy of the Greeley campaign. After-dinner stories gather anecdotes of Whistler, Mark Twain, and President Cleveland. Lives, portraits, and pictures fill a volume built for the parlour table of its day.
69402-twice-round-the-clock-or-the-hours:
Twice Round the Clock is a sketch book of London life by George Sala. Its full title adds the hours of the day and night in London. Wood prints dress the text, with a portrait of the author in front. The book came out in London in the year eighteen sixty two.

Hour by hour the book walks the town from dawn gas light to deep night. Markets, courts, docks, and dens of vice take their turn on the clock face. A warm front letter gives the book to a friend of long years. Bright talk and sharp sight mark the press style of the age. The whole forms a famed guide to the pulse of the great town.
73310-the-printers-stationers-and-bookbi:
E Gordon Duff wrote The Printers, Stationers and Bookbinders of Westminster and London from fourteen seventy six to fifteen thirty five. The book holds his Sandars Lectures of eighteen ninety nine and nineteen four, issued at Cambridge at the University Press in nineteen six. Duff was sometime Sandars Reader in Bibliography. He dedicated the book to Francis John Henry Jenkinson.

Six plates, full size of the originals, illustrate it. A title page to W de Worde edition of the Book of Good Manners faces page thirty six. A Machlinia border used by R Pynson faces page fifty six. A page of the Sarum Breviary printed at Venice in fourteen eighty three follows. A binding of Frederick Egmont on a Rouen printed book is shown. An unrecorded device used by W de Worde in fifteen two also appears. Book historians get the standard study of early English printing trades.
74563-a-new-practical-and-easy-method-of:
A New Practical and Easy Method of Learning the Portuguese Language is a grammar printed at London in 1857. It follows the system of Professor Ahn of the College of Neuss. Franz Thimm, a foreign publisher in Brook Street, issued it. Ahn's grammars for German, French, Italian, and other tongues had already won wide use.

The preface gives the method in one line: learn a foreign language as you learned your mother tongue. A mother repeats the same words a hundred times until the child speaks. So the book builds speech by small steps, starting with how the sounds are said. To study in this way, the editor claims, is no longer study but amusement.
9908-the-false-faces-further-adventures-:
Louis Joseph Vance's 1918 novel continues the adventures of the Lone Wolf, the gentleman thief turned wartime agent. It opens with a man crawling through the mud of No Man's Land, and follows him from a British port into the barred zone, deep waters, and suspicion.

Later chapters place him in a stateroom, off Nantucket, and under the sea, as false faces multiply and no identity can be trusted. Vance writes fast, cinematic adventure in the shadow of the Great War. Fans of gentleman-crook tales get a hero using old skills for a new, patriotic fight.
9920-the-garden-of-bright-waters-one-hun:
Edward Powys Mathers translated this 1920 gathering of one hundred and twenty love poems from across Asia. The poems come from Afghanistan, Persia, and other lands, in forms such as the ghazal and the ballade, with a translator's notes to guide English readers.

Voices praise beloveds, lament parting, and celebrate beauty in short, polished verses, from the Princess of Qulzum to songs of Muhammad Khan. Mathers keeps the poems musical and direct. The book opens a wide, little-known field of Asian poetry to readers who know only European love lyrics.
britannica-1911-stewart-julius-l:
Julius L Stewart was an American artist born in Philadelphia in eighteen fifty five. His short life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father William Hood Stewart collected fine art and backed early work by Fortuny and the Barbizon painters. The family later lived in Paris, where art shaped the son from youth.

Stewart trained under Gerome at the Ecole des Beaux Arts and under Raymondo de Madrazo. The entry names four key works to show his range and his buyers. They are The Hunt Ball, Full Speed, Five o clock Tea, and Court in Cairo. Readers get a brief guide to a painter tied to rich patrons on both sides of the sea.
cecilia-de-noe-l:
Lanoe Falconer's novel, issued by Macmillan in a 1910 edition, opens after dinner with Atherley preaching his gospel: there is no revelation but that of science. Bread, not manna, is his offer — fact over fancy, daylight over stained glass. His wife knits through the sermon. The narrator, Lyndsay, is too tired to answer.

Talk of that kind, in drawing rooms and country houses, forms the book's real action. Faith, doubt, and the hope of something beyond the seen world are argued by people who feel the stakes personally. Cecilia stands at the still centre of the debate. Falconer writes a quiet novel of belief, where a household's small disorders sit beside very large questions.
doe-osti-17120800-analytical-and-numeric:
Trevor Taylor of Los Alamos models a simple two wire transmission line ending in an inductive load, in a report issued 1 October 2026. The line is treated as lossless, with parallel copper wires in air. Both time behavior and frequency behavior are worked out, so the two views can be checked against each other.

In the time domain, the Telegrapher equations are marched with a staggered leapfrog finite difference scheme. A special implicit update at the load keeps the voltage from blowing up. In the frequency domain, phasor formulas give voltage and current along the line, plus input impedance and natural resonance frequencies. A broadband Gaussian pulse test up to 600 megahertz confirms the numerical results match the analytical ones.
doe-osti-2571057-randomized-algorithms-f:
Final report DE-SC0022251, by Per-Gunnar Martinsson of the University of Texas at Austin and dated July 4, 2025, covers a project on randomized algorithms for matrix computations. Such computations sit inside most large scientific simulations, from low-rank approximations of huge matrices to compact forms of the global operators that physics codes produce. Random sampling can shrink these problems before they are solved.

Three lines of work are reported. A hybrid approach to randomized dimension reduction mixes the best traits of older methods. New compression schemes handle rank-structured matrices, including the first method that is both fully black box and strictly linear in run time. The third line builds after-the-fact error checks, using randomized norm estimates that can bound the error with failure odds near one in ten billion. The algorithms proved especially fast on graphics processors and on data too large for memory.
doe-osti-2573744-early-stages-in-the-lif:
Final technical report DE-SC0021004, from Pennsylvania State University under Jerry Y. Harrington, with Israel Silber of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory as original investigator, covers September 2020 to August 2024. Polar skies host widespread stratiform clouds that hold liquid water despite the cold. These mixed-phase clouds push hard on the surface energy budget and on sea ice. Their long, steady middle stage is well studied; their first hours are not.

The project targeted those early stages, when a cloud forms in a calm, stable layer and then either grows turbulent and persists or fades. Data came from the MOSAiC Arctic drift campaign, the AWARE campaign in Antarctica, and the permanent ARM site at Utqiagvik, Alaska. The team found a common formation route earlier work had missed, and measured bulk ice fall at cloud base. They also built a satellite cloud-type product, PHACT, from spaceborne lidar, calibrated on Arctic ground data.
doe-osti-2589599-model-based-hierarchica:
Nathan Shoman prototypes a learning agent that helps design physical protection for guarded sites, in Sandia report SAND2025-11642R. Earlier work built an adversary agent that learned the weakest path through a facility, reacting to its position, to whether it had been spotted, and to side targets. Static graph tools cannot adapt that way.

The new direction is a planning agent that works like autocomplete for security designers. It respects walls and sensors a human expert has already placed and suggests what might come next. Training data came from maze generators, and a variational autoencoder learned to blend maze styles into new layouts between the two. The prototype is not production-ready: the adversary agent still generalizes poorly and trains slowly. The report records both the promise and those limits.
doe-osti-2997628-equilibrium-isotope-fra:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-29871, by Kirill Velizhanin, issued 3 October 2025, adds isotope sorting to the laboratory's Magpie code. Sorting, called fractionation, is the slight split of heavy and light isotopes between phases at balance, driven by mass gaps in how molecules vibrate. The effect marks where materials have been and how they were made.

Theory chapters build the tools: ideal mixing, partition functions for one molecule split into shift, spin, and shake parts, and the beta factor that sums up the sorting strength. Code results are checked against published data. Most of the gaps left trace to the input frequencies and spin constants, with non-harmonic effects adding a smaller share. Users in forensics and earth science gain a checked tool, not a black box.
doe-osti-3005213-analytical-estimates-of:
V. Smaluk and A. Khan of Brookhaven estimate beam limits in technical note BNL-229164-2025-TECH, dated November 2025. The machine is the Beam Accumulator Ring, part of the Electron-Ion Collider injector chain. The ring stacks up a polarized electron beam, one bunch carrying up to 28 nanocoulombs, before handing it to the rapid cycling synchrotron and then the storage ring.

The authors model longitudinal and transverse collective effects with a broadband impedance model, calibrated against beam measurements from the old NSLS VUV ring. They assess microwave and transverse mode-coupling instabilities, bunch lengthening, and beam heating from resistive walls and cavity shapes. Analytical estimates like these set the design envelope early, before the ring exists to measure. Exceeding them in operation would mean lost beam, so the injector design keeps margin against each limit.
doe-osti-3013256-the-lift-community-of-p:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5000-94895, by Weston Eaton, Shweta Iyer, Julia Talamo, and four co-authors, dated December 2025, collects the 2024 lessons of the LIFT Community of Practice. LIFT brings together people working where offshore wind development meets coastal and fishing communities. The community of practice format lets practitioners trade methods rather than each solving the same problems alone.

The 2024 activities included a foresighting workshop with fishing communities. Participants set out needs such as preserving fishing permits and training for the next generation, better local access to seafood, and secure rights to ocean space shared with new uses. Facilitators then linked those needs to concrete strategies, including fisheries mitigation funds. The report distills what the network learned for groups designing similar engagement work.
doe-osti-3013450-satellite-based-investi:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4395, by Matt McCarthy, David Hughes, Shannon Meade, and five co-authors, presents SILVANUS, a satellite-based investigation of vegetation growing into power lines across the United States. Trees touching lines cause outages and spark fires, and utilities now walk or fly thousands of miles of corridor to find trouble spots. The project tested whether satellites can do that scouting instead.

The team built mapping pipelines for two kinds of imagery: multispectral WorldView pictures and synthetic aperture radar, which sees through cloud. Output maps were scored against NOAA validation maps at random sample points. One of the three test maps carried too much cloud cover for valid statistics and was dropped. The report records accuracy results and a clearance verification method for utility vegetation programs.
doe-osti-3014640-apex-study-compensating:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-229314-2026-TECH, by A. Singh, S. Mai, K. Mernick, and F. Severino, dated January 2026, reports an APEX study on compensating transient beam loading in RHIC's 28 megahertz cavities. The coming Electron-Ion Collider will collide beams up to 2.5 amperes, three times RHIC's current, and those currents will yank cavity voltages around, risking beam loss. The team rehearsed countermeasures on the existing machine.

New firmware and software include a digital network analyzer built into the low-level radio frequency system, which characterizes the cavity loop without hardware changes. One-turn feedback then cuts the effective cavity impedance by a typical 30 decibels across up to eight harmonics. Using the analyzer and a model-based tuner, the team pinned the feedback loop delay at about 2.1 microseconds.
doe-osti-3017156-coupled-cvd-and-float-z:
K L Schulte of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this February 2026 final technical report, NLR/TP-5K00-94861. It models a new reactor for making photovoltaic-grade silicon. Today's silicon comes from pulling single crystal boules from polycrystalline feed made by the Siemens process. That route uses very large amounts of energy, and almost all production sits outside the United States.

The proposed design couples chemical vapor deposition with a float zone reactor in one unit. Modeling explored how operating choices move crystal growth rates. Narrower channels led to higher growth rates. Argon inflow effects were less tidy, giving very low or very high growth depending on reactor pressure. The boule-to-wall gap also mattered somewhat. A working version promises cheaper, more efficient silicon wafers with less energy, and a path to making them domestically.
doe-osti-3018734-databook-inputs-to-safe:
Sandia's Space Nuclear Systems Launch Safety Group issued this databook guide, SAND2026-16497R, in January 2026. Daniel J Clayton and Brian D Ehrhart are the named authors. Launching a nuclear power system requires a full safety analysis, and that analysis is only as good as its inputs. The guide defines exactly which data a mission must hand over. Mission goals and launch window dates come first. The window matters because it fixes the weather conditions the analysis must consider.

Vehicle data follow: configuration, component dimensions, relative locations, and materials. Propellant types and amounts set the blast and thermal environments. Flight termination system details shape the accident sequences worth modeling. Later sections work through accident-initiating events and the outcome conditions where the nuclear system first meets a damaging environment. For mission teams, the databook turns an open-ended safety review into a checklist with named deliverables.
doe-osti-3374724-advancing-artificial-in:
A short technical report for Department of Energy funding call 0002705 sums up artificial intelligence work for liquid argon neutrino detectors. David Caratelli led the project at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Xiao Luo served as co-investigator. The host detectors are liquid argon time projection chambers. They image neutrino events as fine three-dimensional pictures, and sorting those pictures is a hard pattern problem.

One result brought Optimal Transport into this detector type for the first time. The method, borrowed from collider data work, separates neutral pion background from true single electrons. Paired with standard learning tools, it doubled or better the background rejection. A second result put the NuGraph2 graph network to work on real MicroBooNE data. The team fixed a bias in the simulation-trained model, then wired its labels into the standard reconstruction code.
doe-osti-3375079-title-benchmarking-of-h:
A research performance progress report from the University of Illinois team of Deborah Levin Fliflet and D. Levin covers a short project on benchmarking plasma simulation codes. The work links the Illinois CHAOS code with codes at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory. CHAOS is a fully kinetic, three-dimensional code for plasma plumes. It was first built for unmagnetized flows, the kind made by electric thrusters.

During the project the team added magnetic field effects to CHAOS. That upgrade lets it model magnetized nozzles both in space and in test chambers. The science focus is electron cooling as a plume expands along field lines. The team asks which field strengths and densities let a polytropic law stand in for full physics. It also weighs how electron collisions with ions and neutrals change the flow. A 2025 journal paper by Vatansever and Levin reports the code work.
doe-osti-3547205-evaluating-microchannel:
Sandia report SAND2026-25296, printed March 2026, evaluates microchannel heat exchanger lifetime for concentrated solar power. Matthew Sandlin leads an eleven-author team from Sandia, Lockheed Martin, VPE Thermal, and the Electric Power Research Institute. These compact exchangers face high heat and pressure in solar plants.

Past uniaxial tests broke samples, but pressurized samples in one study never failed. That gap blocks lifetime models based on complex service stresses. Stress field shifts can move failure to unexpected spots. Plant designers need pressure-true test data before trusting any lifetime claims for these exchangers.
doe-osti-3943099-discovering-tunable-reg:
Nine Sandia National Laboratories staff, from David Montes de Oca Zapiain and Dennis C. Robinson Brown to Tina M. Nenoff, report a search for porous liquids that can be tuned and reused. Their report, SAND2026-26473R, was printed in September 2026. A porous liquid flows like a fluid yet holds tiny cages that can trap gas.

Machine learning guides the hunt, screening cage and solvent pairs before lab work begins. The report lists journal papers the project produced, among them a 2026 study on tuning carbon dioxide uptake in covalent organic frameworks by adding metals such as copper, manganese, and zinc. Staff and student work gets its own section. A liquid that soaks up gas, gives it back on demand, and flows through pipes could ease carbon capture and gas storage alike.
doe-osti-7315387-vapor-pressure-of-vario:
G. A. Burrell and I. W. Robertson measured the vapor pressures of many compounds at low temperatures for the U.S. Bureau of Mines, in Technical Paper 142, printed in Washington in 1916. Vapor pressure tells how fast a substance turns to gas at a given cold. Mines and gas plants of the day needed such numbers for safe handling of light gases.

The pair froze each compound and read its pressure as it warmed step by step. Nitrous oxide, for one, stayed liquid down to a set point and turned solid below it. From the readings they drew vapor pressure curves with the aid of an empirical formula credited to Nernst. Tables give the raw results for each compound. Chemists who work with cold gases still need this kind of base data, and the paper shows the care early labs took to get it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BakerMarionL_Ba: Marion L. Baker was the Dallas motorcycle officer who, minutes after the shots, ran into the Texas School Book Depository. There he confronted Lee Harvey Oswald in the second-floor lunchroom, the only face-to-face meeting between Oswald and authority before his arrest. Baker let him go when the building manager vouched for him as an employee. This file holds the government material filed under Baker's name in the assassination records, kept as issued.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ErnstMorrisL_Er:
Harrison E. Salisbury wrote in The Nation on December 1, 1984 about a friendship that puzzled many people. Morris Ernst, a leading civil liberties lawyer, and J. Edgar Hoover, the FBI director, corresponded for twenty-five years. Salisbury counted some 300 letters between 1939 and 1964 and called the exchange a strange correspondence.

Ernst defended free speech for a living, while Hoover's Bureau watched and filed away dissenters. Their long, friendly letters cut against both men's public images. Salisbury works through what the two men wrote to each other, and the article itself stands as the record of that unlikely tie.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WadeHarveyL_Wad: nsia-WadeHarveyL Wade Harvey L: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeinbergRobertL: Three lawyers ran for president-elect of the D.C. Bar, and short biographies present each candidate. The sketches are filed under the name Robert L. Weinberg. Bar elections decide who leads the legal profession in the capital, and voters got these brief career summaries to judge by. The set preserves the candidates as their peers saw them: training, posts held, and standing in Washington law.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WideWorldLectur: Harold Weisberg wrote to Selma Warner at the Wide World Lecture Bureau on October 24, 1971. Lecture bureaus booked speakers for colleges and civic groups, and Weisberg lectured on the Kennedy assassination. The letter belongs to the business side of his public campaign. It shows a researcher arranging talks, dates, and terms while his fight with the official story continued in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WirinAL_Wirin_A: Harold Weisberg opened a letter to A. L. Wirin on February 25, 1973, by calling himself a voice from the past. Wirin was a noted civil liberties lawyer in Los Angeles. Weisberg kept ties with lawyers who had crossed his path over the years. The letter preserves one such renewal of contact, written in his familiar direct style.
his-grace-of-osmonde-being-the-portions-:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this novel as the mate to A Lady of Quality. Its title says it gives the parts of the Duke of Osmonde's life left out of his lady's tale. The hosted copy was printed in 1914, from an 1897 copyright. The story opens in April 1676.

Osmonde grows from boy lord to duke amid court scandal and wagers. Clo Wildairs, wild and famed, stands at the tale's heart. Duels of wit, sold portraits, and Thames rescues fill the chapters. Readers get a rich costume romance of Restoration England, told from the hero's side.
lady-bridget-in-the-never-never-land-a-s:
Rosa Praed published Lady Bridget in the Never-Never Land in 1915. Its subtitle calls it a story of Australian life. The book is told from three points of view.

Mrs. Gildea narrates the first part from her cottage study. Her home overlooks the broad Leichardt River at Emu Point. Lady Bridget O'Hara tells the second part in her own voice. Colin McKeith and others carry the third. Shifting narrators let Praed contrast English manners with rough bush life in Australia's far north. Place names and river scenes anchor the romance in Queensland's north. Praed knew that country from her own long residence there.
libraries-in-the-medieval-and-renaissanc:
John Willis Clark delivered this Rede Lecture at Cambridge on June 13, 1894. Macmillan and Bowes published it that year. Clark was the university's registrary and a former fellow of Trinity College.

Lantern slides illustrated the lecture as he spoke. A frontispiece shows part of the chained library at Zutphen. Clark begins by asking what a library may be considered. He then traces libraries through medieval and Renaissance centuries. Monks, colleges, and princes built the collections he describes. Zutphen's chained books still survive for visitors today. Clark uses such survivals to make medieval libraries tangible.
nasa-tm-19680018138-quantitative-analysi:
Gilbert Boyd and David E. Kuivinen of Lewis Research Center present a method for analyzing rocket exhaust products in this 1967 conference paper. The exhaust came from burning liquid oxygen with liquid hydrogen. Knowing exactly what leaves the nozzle helps engineers judge engine performance.

The paper was prepared for the Interagency Chemical Rocket Propulsion Group meeting at Canoga Park in May 1967. A spectrometer supplied the quantitative analysis of the combustion products. The authors describe how the products were measured and counted. Their approach supports careful checks of how completely the propellants burn. It also gives engine testers a tool for comparing runs and designs.
nasa-tm-19700026497-visibility-of-lunar-:
NASA staff prepared this study of crater visibility during the landing module's final approach. A pilot coming down to the Moon must judge the ground by the craters he can see. The study asks which crater sizes a pilot can detect at each point on the way in.

The data are given as raw plots rather than smoothed claims. For each point, the visible area is analyzed and the smallest detectable crater is found. Those sizes are plotted on a map, with lines drawn between size ranges. The work treats craters as round bowls with a fixed depth ratio. It leaves human factors aside on purpose.
paris-france-officialite-paris-france-of:
A sentence of the Officialité of Paris condemns a book in this 1688 document. The book is the Roman Breviary translated into French. Denis Thierry printed it in Paris, finishing on November 15, 1687. The court's promoter appeared at the audience of Saturday, March 13. He complained of both the printing and the version. François Muguet, printer to the King and the Archbishop, printed the sentence itself.

The charges are stated plainly in the French text. Councils, edicts, and royal ordinances forbid printing such translations. The version contains propositions that are erroneous and suspect. Some are contrary to the faith itself. Others endanger the salvation of souls. The document is a small, sharp artifact of Gallican censorship. Rome's breviary in French was itself treated as a crime.
rowdy-of-the-cross-l:
B. M. Sinclair, also known as B. M. Bower, wrote Rowdy of the Cross L, a western tale in thirteen chapters. The contents move from Lost in a Blizzard and Miss Conroy Refuses Shelter to Rowdy Hires a New Boss and At Home at Cross L. Later chapters include A Shot from the Dark, Moving the Herd, Harry Conroy at Home, and Rowdy Promoted. The tale closes with You Can Tell Jessie and Rowdy Finds Happiness, a plan that pairs ranch work and danger with a love interest.

Chapter 1 finds Rowdy Vaughan lost in a blizzard, and far from happy about it. Christened Rowland by his mother, he was renamed Rowdy by cowboy friends who treat mothers' names with little respect. He stands in the stirrups to shake thick, damp snow from his long coat and gray hat, then settles back with a shiver.
the-book-bills-of-narcissus-an-account-r: Richard Le Gallienne wrote The Book-Bills of Narcissus, put out in 1895 with a front plate by Robert Fowler. The chapter list runs from two opening parts and Narcissus with his bag to Accounts Rendered. An Idyll of Alice Sunshine, The Sibylline Books, and The Children of Apollo follow. George Muncaster and That Thirteenth Maid close the list. A note says this third form of the book was worked over, and that the fifth chapter is new. A verse gift to Mildred, dated December 6, 1894, stands before the text.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Artemus Ward's London Punch letters are the promised matter of part 5, per a record title that itself breaks off. Behind the Ward mask stands Charles Farrar Browne. The Gutenberg header is the whole of what is present, legal notices and all. None of the Punch writing follows, so its humor cannot be judged from what is given.
the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-1-janua: The Continental Monthly, a Boston magazine devoted to literature and national policy, is shown here through the title page and index of its first volume, dated 1862. James R. Gilmore entered the volume for copyright in 1861, with Boston and New York sellers named on the title page. The index lists Horace Greeley's Across the Continent, Edmund Kirke's Among the Pines, and C. G. Leland on early Norse finders of America. Only the volume front matter and index are present here, rather than the January issue's own pages.
the-continental-monthly-vol-4-no-4-octob: October 1863 brings the fourth number of volume IV of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its contents list The Freedom of the Press, a life of astrologer William Lilly, a piece on Jefferson Davis, and Thirty Days with the Seventy-First Regiment. Poems, a detective's story, chapters of two serial tales, and pieces on currency and American finances round out the list, with literary notices at the end. Only the masthead, the contents, and the first line of the press article are present here.
the-false-faces-further-adventures-from-: Louis Joseph Vance wrote The False Faces as further tales from the history of the Lone Wolf, dated 1918. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads run from No Man's Land to a British port. They pass through deep waters, a stateroom, and a spot off Nantucket. They end with a dance of death. All this points to a spy and crime tale set in war time, at sea and ashore.
the-garden-of-bright-waters-one-hundred-:
Edward Powys Mathers turned one hundred and twenty Asian love poems into English verse in The Garden of Bright Waters, printed in 1920. He gives the book to his wife.

The contents sort the poems by land. Afghan songs come first: ghazals and ballades by named singers on love and loss. Annam follows with songs of gardens, rivers, and girls waiting to wed students. Arabic pieces close the part that can be read here. Mathers drew on tongues across Asia to show how love sings in many forms, from court ghazal to folk song by a washerman.
the-heart-s-secret-or-the-fortunes-of-a-:
Lieutenant Murray Ballou wrote The Heart's Secret; or, The Fortunes of a Soldier, published in Boston in 1852. A publisher's note says the novelette first ran in the Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion. The contents promise chapters such as The Accident, The Belle and the Soldier, Cuban Banditti, The Wounded Soldier, The Execution Scene, and Happy Finale.

The preface sets the scene in Cuba, called a gem of the American archipelago, with praise for its fields and shores. Ballou links the tale to love and danger in a tropical place, with soldiers, bandits, a queen, and disguise among the turns named in the contents. A second record in the library carries the same publisher's note and preface.
the-roots-of-the-mountains-wherein-is-to: William Morris gave The Roots of the Mountains a long subtitle. It promises the lives of the men of Burgdale, with their friends, neighbours, and foemen. Longmans, Green issued the edition transcribed here in 1896. A first edition appeared in November 1889. The pages at hand give the title and a verse epigraph. They also give the first contents entries only. The tale itself is not shown. Early chapters introduce Burgstead and its folk. Then comes Face-of-god and his kindred.
the-vision-of-sir-launfal-and-other-poem: James Russell Lowell's Vision of Sir Launfal and Other Poems appears in the Riverside Literature Series from Houghton, Mifflin, with a portrait and other illustrations. The title page promises a biographical sketch and notes alongside the poems. Copyright lines run from 1848 through 1896. The material present here stops at the contents of that biographical sketch, so Lowell's poems do not appear. Sketch sections are titled Elmwood, Education, First Ventures, Verse and Prose, and Public Life.
thirty-one-years-on-the-plains-and-in-th:
Capt. William F. Drannan claimed an authentic record of thirty-one years hunting, trapping, scouting, and fighting on the far western plains. He went west at fifteen. His preface insists the book is plain narration, not romance or fine literature.

The preface summarises a boyhood flight to St. Louis, a meeting with Kit Carson, and a first plains trip. Fremont, Beckwith, and Jim Bridger appear among his companions, and generals Crook and Connor among his later commanders. Readers get a frontiersman's life story that also sketches how western cities sprang into existence.
yorkshire-tales-third-series-amusing-ske: John Hartley wrote these amusing sketches of Yorkshire life in Yorkshire dialect, gathered as a third series. Pages present here hold the title page, a cheerful verse motto about forgiving and forgetting, and a contents list. Sketch titles include Grimes' New Hat, Sammywell Sweeps th' Chimley, and Sheffield Smook. A factory romance called True Blue also appears. The sketches themselves do not appear in these pages, beyond titles and motto.
